Question 47. Probability that two ranks are ever compared

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

In ideal randomized quicksort with distinct ranks, find the probability that ranks three and eight are compared. Why are pivots outside this interval irrelevant to the event?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The rank interval contains six records: three through eight. The pair remains together until a pivot from that interval is selected. A pivot outside it puts both ranks into the same child and cannot separate them. If the first selected interval rank is three or eight, that pivot is compared with the other endpoint. If it is four through seven, the endpoints enter different children and never meet again. All six ranks are equally likely to be first under uniform random priorities, so the probability is 2/6=1/3. The argument depends on sorted ranks, not their physical original indices.

Question 48. Balanced expectation can conceal one-sided executions

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The two possible splits are (0,n-1) and (n-1,0), so each labeled child has mean length (n-1)/2. Nevertheless every execution has one nonempty child of length n-1. With a linear partition toll, the recurrence is T(n)=T(n-1)+Θ(n), giving Θ(n2). Selecting the extremes by an extra linear scan keeps that same order. The invalid step is replacing E[T(|L|)] with T(E[|L|]). Balanced means describe no actual execution here. The correct uniform-pivot analysis averages over every rank or uses pair indicators, rather than analyzing an imagined average-sized split.

Question 49. Probability of a completely extreme pivot chain

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

For five distinct keys with independent uniform pivot choices in each current range, find the probability of choosing an extreme rank at every nontrivial call.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

At range size m≥2, exactly two of the m ranks are extremes. Conditional on all previous choices being extreme, only one nontrivial child remains, of size m-1. Multiply conditional probabilities: (2/5)(2/4)(2/3)(2/2)=2/15. In general the probability is ∏m=2n2/m=2n-1/n!. Every such execution has the maximal ideal comparison sum n(n-1)/2. The small probability does not make worst-case time disappear, nor does it justify claiming that a randomized execution always meets a fixed deadline. This event calculation assumes distinct keys and the stated uniform conditional choices.

Question 50. Median of three is a local rank promise

Read the complete solution and reasoning

One sampled record is below the median and one above, so the pivot's zero-based global rank lies between one and n-2. There is no stronger guarantee from only these three records: every unsampled record can be above the pivot, making one child length one and the other n-2. Question 52. Exact-median pivot gives a worst-case guarantee

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Assume a deterministic linear-time exact-median subroutine and partition preserving distinct records. Derive the full quicksort worst-case runtime, including median computation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Median finding and partition together cost Θ(n) per range. The exact median gives children of lengths ⌊(n-1)/2⌋ and ⌈(n-1)/2⌉. Therefore T(n)=T(⌊(n-1)/2⌋)+T(⌈(n-1)/2⌉)+Θ(n), whose balanced tree has logarithmic depth and linear work per level, giving Θ(nlogn). Question 53. Smaller-first is insufficient without tail iteration

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

An implementation recursively sorts the smaller child first and then recursively sorts the larger child. Does this guarantee logarithmic stack depth on one-sided partitions? State the correct transformation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. When one child is empty, its recursive call returns immediately, but the larger child is still entered recursively while the parent activation remains live. Repeating yields a chain of linear many active calls. Instead recurse only on the smaller child and handle the larger child by updating bounds in a loop inside the current activation. Every actual nested recursive call then enters a range of size at most half the preceding range, so there are O(logn) simultaneous activations even on a quadratic-time pivot history. Merely ordering recursive calls does not remove the parent frame. Runtime and storage guarantees must be proved independently.

Question 54. Timing evidence cannot alone prove an exponent

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

When the input size is multiplied by four, one measured sorting time grows about fivefold and another about eightfold. A researcher declares exact nlogn and n2 laws. What can be inferred, and what remains unproved?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

If an exact dominant cnlog2n law applied, the ratio would be 4(1+2/log2n), tending toward four. An exact dominant cn2 law would give sixteen, not eight. The observations can motivate hypotheses, but constants, lower-order terms, measurement setup, caching and input families can distort finite ratios. Big-O alone does not assert equality with one monomial. Under the special promise that two known implementations differ only in fixed-first versus random pivot and are tested on sorted distinct inputs, relative degradation can help identify the fixed-pivot implementation, but still is not a general asymptotic proof. Derive the recurrence from the algorithm before claiming a Theta law.

Use the taught early-stop sink on seven equal keys. Find construction and total comparison counts, and explain why this does not contradict heapsort's worst-case bound.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Each of the three internal nodes has two children, so construction makes two comparisons at each and stops immediately: six. After each root/end exchange, active lengths are six, five, four, three, two and one. Root sinking then uses two, two, two, two, one and zero comparisons, totaling nine. The whole execution has fifteen comparisons and six nontrivial root/end swaps, with no downward swaps. Keys being equal makes every parent pass the early-stop condition. Worst-case Θ(nlogn) means there exist inputs requiring that order, not that every input has it. The specified all-equal family takes linear work.

All-equal heapsort can be linear

Question 65. Heap order does not preserve equal identities

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Heapsort [2a,2b,1c] with the taught max-heap code. Is the result stable? Why does initially valid heap order not resolve the question?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The initial array is already a max-heap, so construction leaves it alone. Moving the root 2a to the last slot gives [1c,2b,2a]. Sinking the one swaps it with 2b, giving [2b,1c,2a]. The final extraction yields [1c,2b,2a]. Equal identities are reversed, so this method is not stable. Heap order constrains parent keys versus child keys and says nothing about original chronological order among equals. A valid heap can therefore be the starting point of an unstable sortdown. Decorating keys with original indices can enforce the target order but changes the comparison and storage model.

Question 66. An integer decision-tree lower bound

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

What integer worst-comparison lower bound follows from sorting six distinct keys using binary pair comparisons? Does that prove a sorter attaining the bound exists?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The tree needs at least 6!=720 leaves. Since 29=512<720≤1024=210, its height is at least ten. The conclusion is a lower bound: every correct tree must have some path of at least ten comparisons. It does not construct an attainable sorting tree, and arbitrary balanced binary questions might not be legal pairwise comparisons of records. Nor does it say every input takes ten comparisons. To prove optimality for a small fixed size, a legal sorting construction and a matching lower bound are both needed.

Question 67. Multiplicity changes the leaf count

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Known key multiplicities are four, two and two in eight slots. Compute the distinct-arrangement count and binary-comparison leaf lower bound; compare with all-distinct keys.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The count is 8!/(4!2!2!)=420. Binary height is at least ⌈log2420⌉=9, because 256<420≤512. With eight distinct keys, the count is 8!=40320 and the corresponding bound is sixteen. Equal keys reduce the number of possible key arrangements; labeled record identities still matter for stability but do not create additional unknown key orders inside a known equal group. The model counts binary decisions; a primitive three-outcome comparison can require a different constant-base branching calculation on inputs with ties. Bounds apply to the stated input family and primitive.

Question 68. Merging has less unknown order than sorting

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Two internally sorted distinct runs have lengths two and six. Explain the (82) arrangement count and why the unrestricted 8! sorting count is wrong.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The internal order of each run is already fixed. An output is determined by choosing the two positions occupied by records from the first run; the other six positions are filled by the second run in its known order. Thus there are (82)=28 possible interleavings, not 8!. The binary leaf lower bound is five comparisons. Applying an unrestricted distinct sorting bound would count internal run permutations that the precondition excludes. Ordinary merging can still use seven comparisons on a worst supplied interleaving. Information lower bounds constrain the best possible worst-case strategy, while the cost of one particular strategy can be larger.

Question 69. Lower-bound quantifiers and a sorted input

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

An examiner states: every comparison sorter must use Ω(nlogn) time on an already sorted input. Refute the statement with a correct algorithm and state the valid bound.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Insertion sort with a strict predecessor test checks each new record against its immediate predecessor, makes n-1 key comparisons, shifts nothing and completes in linear time on ascending input. It is nevertheless a correct sorter for arbitrary inputs, with a quadratic worst case. The valid theorem says every correct comparison sorter has a worst-case input family requiring Ω(nlogn) comparisons when arbitrary distinct relative orders are allowed. The theorem does not specify that the hard input is ascending, nor claim that every input is hard. A supplied promise that the input is already sorted can reduce the task further; reading or verification requirements must then be stated.

Question 70. Randomness cannot erase the general average lower bound

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

A randomized comparison sorter is always correct. Outline why some fixed distinct-key input must require expected Ω(nlogn) comparisons.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Fix a sequence of random coins. The resulting correct deterministic sorting tree must distinguish all n! relative input orders. Under a uniform distribution over them, average leaf depth is at least log2(n!). Average that inequality over the algorithm's random coins, exchanging the finite input average and expectation. The average across fixed input orders of their expected costs remains at least log2(n!). At least one fixed input must therefore have an expected cost no smaller than that average. This is a lower bound for always-correct comparison sorting; it does not contradict a randomized algorithm having matching expected upper bounds on every fixed input.

Question 71. An unsorted tail does not require sorting the prefix again

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

A million records contain a known sorted prefix and one thousand arbitrary trailing records. Give a stability-preserving comparison strategy and its asymptotic expression.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Stably sort the thousand-record tail, using O(1000log21000) work, then perform a stable left-first merge with the known sorted prefix in O(106) work. More generally the expression is O(n+klogk) for a tail of size k. The known prefix reduces the unknown-order family, so the unrestricted comparison lower bound is not a barrier. If the records carry payloads, use complete records in the tail sort and output merge. Applying counting sort based solely on the record count would need an additional bounded-integer-key promise; it is not implied by the sorted-prefix information.

Question 72. Stable cumulative scatter positions

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Count-sort records [3a,1b,3c,0d,2e,1f] in universe zero through three. Compute frequencies, cumulative ends and the final identity order.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Frequencies are F=[1,2,1,2], whose cumulative ends are P=[1,3,4,6]. Scanning right to left, 1f goes to slot two, 2e to three, 0d to zero, 3c to five, 1b to one, and 3a to four. Output is [0d,1b,1f,2e,3a,3c]. Each block receives exactly its frequency count; decrementing ends cannot overlap adjacent blocks. The later equal record takes the later slot first, so original equal order survives. All six output writes place distinct original records, while counter updates are separate storage operations rather than key comparisons.

Question 73. A mixed scatter convention reverses ties

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Use cumulative end positions but traverse [2a,1b,2c,1d] left to right, decrementing the end for each record. What identity order results, and how can the convention be repaired?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Frequencies are two ones and two twos, with exclusive ends two and four. Left-to-right traversal places 2a at three, 1b at one, 2c at two and 1d at zero. Output is [1d,1b,2c,2a], reversing both equal groups. To repair it while retaining ends, traverse the original records right to left. To retain left-to-right traversal instead, compute starting positions zero and two and increment them after each placement. Both corrected conventions give [1b,1d,2a,2c]. The off-by-one is not merely numerical: traversal direction and pointer direction jointly establish stability.

Question 74. Negative keys need the range width

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Stably count-sort [-3a,2b,-1c,2d,-3e] with interval [-3,2]. What counter array size is required and what is the final identity order?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The inclusive width is 2-(-3)+1=6. Shift each key by subtracting L=-3: indices are zero, five, two, five, zero. Frequencies are [2,0,1,0,0,2] and cumulative ends are [2,2,3,3,3,5]. Right-to-left scatter gives [-3a,-3e,-1c,2b,2d]. Allocating only three counters because the maximum is two ignores negative indices and the full interval width. Stability preserves both pairs of equal identities. Shifting changes representation used for indexing, not the actual payload or key that must be returned.

Question 75. Sparse occupancy does not shrink a dense universe

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

There are one thousand records but only four occupied key values, all inside an interval of width one billion. Is ordinary dense counting sorting linear in one thousand? What extra work appears in a sparse replacement?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Ordinary dense counting initializes and scans one billion counters, so its cost is Θ(n+K) and its storage includes K, despite only four occupied values. A sparse map can record frequencies or FIFO record groups for the four keys in near-linear scanning time under an appropriate dictionary model. To emit them in ascending key order, the occupied keys must themselves be ordered, for example by comparing and sorting those four keys; dictionary iteration is not automatically ordered. If the number of distinct keys varies, this gives a distinct-value sorting term and dictionary assumptions. Low occupancy and small universe are different conditions, and neither alone eliminates representation cost.

Question 76. Counts-only reconstruction loses payloads

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Oxford B16 counts-only variant versus MIT stable-record variant, independently synthesized problem

A counting routine emits integer key j exactly Fj times. Applied to records (key,name), does it establish a stable record sort? Describe what must be stored instead.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

It reconstructs only the numerical key multiset; names and other attached fields have been discarded. Calling the output stable is therefore meaningless for the original records, and the record permutation contract is violated. Store each complete record in a FIFO key bucket or retain the original array and scatter complete records into cumulative positions. Then prove every occurrence is output exactly once and equality retains original order. If the input really consists solely of indistinguishable integer values, counts-only reconstruction is a legitimate integer sorting variant. The validity depends on the input contract, not on the algorithm's shared counting-sort name.

Question 77. Three exact LSD decimal passes

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

MIT 6.006 Recitation 5 Exercise 1: exact written exercise with independently explained solution

Sort [329,457,657,839,436,720,355] using stable LSD base-ten passes. Give the complete array after each pass and justify the final order.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The units pass yields [720,355,436,457,657,329,839]: equal units seven retain 457 before 657, and equal units nine retain 329 before 839. The tens pass yields [720,329,436,839,355,457,657]: the prior order resolves each equal tens bucket. The hundreds pass yields [329,355,436,457,657,720,839]. After one pass the units are sorted; after two, the two-digit suffix is sorted; after three, every full three-digit key is sorted. Buckets are concatenated in digit order and preserve FIFO identity order. Sorting digits independently without that stability invariant would not justify these arrays.

Question 78. An unstable digit pass invalidates LSD

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

After a stable units pass on [12,11], an unstable tens sorter reverses equal tens. Give the resulting array and identify the broken invariant.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The units pass puts eleven before twelve, giving [11,12], correctly sorted by the low digit. Both tens are one. Reversing that equal tens bucket then produces [12,11], which is not numerically sorted. The next-digit pass must preserve the established lower-suffix order among equal next digits; instability removes precisely that property. It is not enough that each individual digit list appears sorted after its pass. A correct LSD proof compares two keys by the new digit first and, when that digit ties, relies on their previous suffix order. This two-record counterexample isolates the missing condition.

Question 79. Global MSD-then-LSD passes solve the wrong priority

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Globally sort [21,12] first by tens and then stably by units. Does this implement numeric order? Contrast recursive MSD.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The tens pass gives [12,21]. A global units pass then gives [21,12], because one precedes two, so numeric order is lost. The last stable pass becomes the highest-priority key when passes are global. Recursive MSD avoids this by sorting lower digits only within each equal high-digit bucket. Here the tens buckets each contain one record, so no later pass can mix them. The distinction is between refining a fixed high-priority group and reordering the entire array by a lower-priority component. Pass direction alone is not a complete algorithm specification.

Question 80. Inclusive and exclusive universe boundaries

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

With base two, compare digit counts for keys below exclusive U=1024 and keys up to inclusive M=1024. Explain why a floating-log shortcut can be unsafe.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Keys below 1024 have maximum 1023 and need ten binary digits because 210=1024 covers the exclusive universe. The inclusive maximum 1024 itself is binary one followed by ten zeros, so it needs eleven digits. Thus d=⌈log2U⌉ for the first case and d=⌊log2M⌋+1 for the second. Treating the same numeric bound as both inclusive and exclusive gives an off-by-one at exact powers. Floating-point logarithms near a boundary can also round incorrectly; repeated integer division or a tested place-value loop computes the required pass count exactly.

Question 81. A bit-length ratio is not an exact arbitrary-base digit count

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

MIT radix implementation audit: newly authored correction and counterexample

For base B=n=3 and exclusive universe U=59049=310, evaluate 1+⌊bitlength(U)/bitlength(n)⌋. Is that enough passes for key U-1?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The universe 59049 has binary bit length sixteen, while three has bit length two. The proposed expression gives 1+⌊16/2⌋=9. But U-1=59048 has ten base-three digits, all two, and nine passes cannot inspect its highest digit. The ratio of rounded binary lengths is not the exact logarithm in base three. Use the minimum integer d satisfying 3d≥U, which is ten, or repeated integer division. Approximate formulas acceptable for some asymptotic estimates must not become exact implementation bounds without a proof. This independently checked edge case motivated the chapter's explicit digit loop.

Question 82. Linear radix on a shifted polynomial interval

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

MIT Recitation 5 Exercise 2: reconstructed and strengthened with exact boundaries

Design a word-RAM linear-time method for integers in [-n2,n3], with n≥2. Bound the required base- n digits after a monotone shift.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Add n2 to each key, producing nonnegative values at most n3+n2. For n≥2, this maximum is less than n4, so at most four base- n digits suffice. Perform four stable counting digit passes with n counters each, costing O(n+n) per pass and O(n) peak extra storage when buffers are reused. Retain original complete records or subtract the shift after sorting values. The shift is monotone, preserving order. The constant four and the word-size arithmetic assumption are essential; arbitrary huge integers can invalidate a constant-cost operation model. For a singleton, handle the base-one issue by returning directly.

Question 83. Digit width trades memory for passes

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

For a million unsigned 64-bit keys, compare dense radix work estimates with eight-bit and sixteen-bit digits. Explain why thirty-two-bit digits can be infeasible.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Eight-bit digits require eight passes and 256 counters, giving proxy work 8(1000000+256)=8002048. Sixteen-bit digits need four passes and 65536 counters, giving 4(1000000+65536)=4262144. Under this simplified equal-cost proxy the sixteen-bit option is smaller, but actual cache behavior and counter initialization constants still matter. Thirty-two-bit digits need only two passes yet require 232 counters, which is billions of entries and can exceed available memory. The general formula is ⌈64/b⌉(n+2b) with peak buffer plus counter storage, not just the number of passes. A memory constraint can override the arithmetic proxy.

Question 84. Encoded size changes a claimed linear bound

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Keys have up to n bits, and a radix analysis chooses base n. Why must the arithmetic model be specified when reporting O(n2/logn) digit work?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A key needs roughly n/log2n base- n digits, so a hypothetical constant-cost digit pass yields O(n·n/logn) work. But an n -bit key generally spans many ordinary machine words. Treating divisions, shifts or comparisons of the whole key as constant-time assumes an unusually large word or hides big-integer cost. Reading the complete encoded input already involves up to n2 bits. The meaningful complexity must specify word width, digit extraction representation and whether input/output are measured in records, words or bits. The formal digit-count expression can be correct while its advertised machine runtime is unsupported.

Question 85. Nonuniform bucket probabilities determine expected work

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Independently place n records in buckets with probabilities pi. Derive E[∑iNi2] and evaluate uniform placement into n buckets versus one bucket.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Write Ni=∑j=1nXji. Its second moment is npi+n(n-1)pi2, because diagonal terms are Xji and independent distinct-record terms have expectation pi2. Summing and using ∑ipi=1 yields n+n(n-1)∑ipi2. For n uniform buckets, the squared probabilities sum to 1/n, giving 2n-1. For one bucket the sum is one, giving n2. Insertion work within buckets is bounded by this second moment, so independent near-balanced placement can give expected linear time while concentration permits quadratic work. Marginal probabilities alone are insufficient if placements are dependent.

Question 86. A concentrated bucket is a real worst case

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Use five equal intervals for integer percentages zero through ninety-nine, and insertion-sort each bucket. Trace [19,18,17,16,15]. Does bucket assignment make the sort linear?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

All five values lie in the first interval zero through nineteen, so bucket assignment creates one descending five-record bucket and four empty buckets. Its insertion sorter needs (52)=10 strict shifts or adjacent exchanges, with ten successful predecessor comparisons for the specified reverse input. Distribution and concatenation add linear work but do not remove the quadratic internal-sort family when all n inputs similarly concentrate in one bucket. Output is [15,16,17,18,19]. The uniform expected-time theorem assumes a distribution of random placements; one deterministic bucket mapping is not evidence that inputs satisfy it.

Question 87. Strings require an end-of-string order

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

MIT Recitation 5 Exercise 3 and Stanford radix induction: independently extended string problem

Lexicographically sort the strings a, aa, ab, and the empty string. Explain the required MSD sentinel and the character-cost qualification for equal-length strings.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The correct order is empty string, a, aa, ab. The end-of-string sentinel must precede every ordinary character, so a completed string comes before any longer string sharing its prefix. At the first character the empty string enters the terminal bucket; at the next character a enters it before aa and ab. Recursion continues only in nonterminal character buckets. For n equal-length strings of length L over alphabet size R, stable LSD passes cost Θ(L(n+R)), which is linear in all input characters for fixed R, not linear in record count alone. Question 88. External merging counts passes and blocks

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Medium–Hard

Newly authored mathematical/conceptual problem

Let n=106 records, usable buffer memory after metadata M=10000 records, and block size B=100. Generate memory-sized sorted runs, then use one input block per run plus one output block. Compute run count, fan-in, merge passes and total read/write transfers including generation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Run count is r=⌈106/10000⌉=100. The buffer-only fan-in is f=10000/100-1=99, with metadata already excluded as stated. One merge pass reduces one hundred runs to two; the second reduces two to one, so there are two merge passes. Each pass reads and writes all records: 2·10000=20000 transfers. Run generation also reads and writes them once, adding twenty thousand. Total is sixty thousand block transfers under this full-materialization model. CPU head comparisons and final-output omission policies would change other cost terms; they are not included in the stated transfer convention.

20. Final examination rules and transfer notes

Examination rules: conditions, formulas, and failure modes

Rule 1

State the object being sorted before choosing a theorem. A record contains a key and a payload; ordering its key does not authorize losing, duplicating, or reconstructing its payload. Sortedness and multiset preservation are separate obligations.

Rule 2

Stability concerns the order of distinct records with equal keys. The output keys alone cannot establish it. Label equal occurrences by original positions and compare their output positions.

Rule 3

A comparator must define a consistent order. With a strict comparator, irreflexivity and transitivity are essential, and the induced equivalence must be transitive. A cyclic comparator can invalidate partition and merge proofs even when every individual comparison terminates.

Rule 4

Do not assume that a tie-breaking rule makes an unstable implementation stable. Decorating each key with its original index makes all composite keys distinct and forces the desired order, but requires index storage and a comparator that actually reads the index.

Rule 5

For secondary and primary keys, a stable secondary-key sort followed by a stable primary-key sort gives lexicographic order. Reversing the pass order reverses the priority. This same principle underlies LSD radix sorting.

Rule 6

Distinguish a key comparison from a loop-bound test, an assignment, a swap, and a comparator call. One ternary comparator call can correspond to two Boolean key tests. Exact operation questions require the code and the counting convention.

Rule 7

A strict inversion is a pair i<j with Ai>Aj. Equal keys contribute no strict inversion. A swap of an inverted adjacent pair removes exactly one inversion; an arbitrary long-distance swap need not do so.

Rule 8

For the stated selection sort, the comparison count is exactly n(n-1)/2 on every input. This is an exact count, whereas Θ(n2) conceals constants and lower-order terms.

Rule 9

Selection sort has at most n-1 nontrivial swaps, but its comparisons remain quadratic. When record writes dominate comparisons, this tradeoff can matter. Do not infer a linear running time from a linear swap count.

Rule 10

Ordinary selection sort is unstable: moving a distant minimum can carry an earlier equal-key record past a later one. Replacing the final swap with a block shift can preserve stability, but can require quadratic writes.

Rule 11

For a known target permutation with c cycles, the minimum number of unrestricted swaps is n-c. The theorem assumes distinct identities and a fixed target; repeated keys may admit several valid targets.

Rule 12

In insertion sort with shifts, the number of predecessor shifts is exactly the initial inversion count I. Placing the saved key adds another write for each of the n-1 outer iterations in the stated implementation, even if its position does not change.

Rule 13

Let r count positions after the first that are strict new prefix minima. With short-circuit testing of the boundary before comparing keys, insertion comparisons equal I+(n-1)-r. Counting a sentinel comparison instead changes this formula.

Rule 14

Insertion sort is stable when it shifts only keys strictly greater than the saved key. Shifting equal keys changes their relative order. The distinction is between > and ≥, not between ascending and descending sorting.

Rule 15

For a uniformly random permutation of distinct keys, E[I]=n(n-1)/4. For a multiset with multiplicities mj, the expectation is (n2-∑jmj2)/4. The distribution over labeled arrangements must be stated.

Rule 16

Binary insertion reduces the search comparisons but does not eliminate array shifts. Its worst-case movement remains quadratic. To preserve stability, insert after existing equal keys, using the upper-bound position.

Rule 17

A left rotation of a sorted distinct array by k positions has k(n-k) inversions. Its insertion cost can therefore be quadratic even though the array consists of only two increasing runs.

Rule 18

With a shrinking upper bound and an early-exit flag, bubble sort uses n-1 comparisons on an already sorted nonempty array. Without the flag, it still executes the triangular comparison count.

Rule 19

Bubble sort's number of strict adjacent swaps equals I. Its number of comparisons need not be Θ(n+I): a small key at the right end can travel left only one position per pass, producing quadratic comparisons with only n-1 inversions.

Rule 20

A large key at the left end can travel to the right end in one left-to-right pass. This direction asymmetry explains why two inputs with the same inversion count can have different bubble comparison counts.

Rule 21

An h -sort sorts each residue class modulo h. It need not sort the whole array when h>1. A final gap of one is required by ordinary Shell sort to establish total order.

Rule 22

If n=qh+r with 0≤r<h, the maximum comparisons for separate insertion sorts of the h chains are r(q+12)+(h-r)(q2). This is a single-gap bound, not automatically a tight total bound for a gap sequence.

Rule 23

Earlier Shell passes alter the inputs of later passes. Summing the independent worst cases of all gaps gives an upper bound, but one input may not attain every term. Never present that sum as an exact worst case without a construction.

Rule 24

Shell sort can be unstable even though each individual chain is sorted stably. Records in different residue classes can cross before they share a chain. Its running-time guarantee depends on the complete gap sequence.

Rule 25

Merging two nonempty sorted runs of lengths p,q uses at most p+q-1 ordinary head comparisons and at least min(p,q). If one run is empty, the count is zero. Copying leftover records performs writes but no head comparisons.

Rule 26

A stable merge chooses the left run when head keys are equal. Choosing the right run reverses cross-run ties even if both input runs were individually stable. Stability must hold at every merge.

Rule 27

In a merge, a selected right key smaller than the current left head contributes the number of remaining left keys to the strict cross-inversion count. Equality contributes zero. Within-run inversions must also be counted recursively.

Rule 28

For balanced top-down mergesort with n=2k, the best head-comparison count is (n/2)log2n and the worst is nlog2n-n+1. These formulas describe ordinary merging without a pre-merge boundary shortcut.

Rule 29

For arbitrary n≥1, balanced mergesort's worst count is n⌈log2n⌉-2⌈log2n⌉+1. Unequal leaf depths matter. Do not round the power-of-two formula by replacing the logarithm alone.

Rule 30

Testing whether the last left key is at most the first right key allows a merge to be skipped. On sorted input, one test per internal node gives n-1 comparisons. On unsorted input, these tests add overhead to the ordinary merge count.

Rule 31

A reusable auxiliary array gives linear peak auxiliary storage. Repeatedly allocating temporary arrays can still have linear peak live storage but Θ(nlogn) cumulative allocated volume. Peak space and total allocation are different metrics.

Rule 32

Bottom-up mergesort doubles the run width each pass. A final incomplete run must be bounded by the array length; it is not padded with genuine records. Its output contract includes exact preservation of all records.

Rule 33

Merging runs one at a time into an ever-growing prefix can be quadratic. A balanced merge schedule has logarithmic participation depth per record. Natural mergesort's advantage depends on both the number of initial runs and the scheduling policy.

Rule 34

Reversing a nonincreasing run can reverse equal-key identities. Stable natural merging either detects strictly decreasing runs or handles equal-key groups separately. A sorted-key picture does not reveal this defect.

Rule 35

If every record is displaced by at most k positions, a min-heap of at most k+1 candidates supports O(nlog(k+1)) sorting. The displacement promise is stronger than a vague statement that the input is nearly sorted.

Rule 36

A partition routine's return value must be interpreted from its contract. Lomuto returns a final pivot index; classic Hoare returns a split boundary that need not contain the pivot. Their recursive child intervals are consequently different.

Rule 37

For the stated strict Lomuto partition on [lo,hi), each nonpivot key is compared once and the pivot ends at b. The children are [lo,b) and [b+1,hi). Reincluding b can prevent termination.

Rule 38

Strict Lomuto with all equal keys puts the pivot at the left edge on every call. It makes n(n-1)/2 comparisons. Randomizing which equal record is chosen does not repair this key-value imbalance.

Rule 39

Classic Hoare scans must stop on equality and advance after exchanges. Otherwise equal keys can cause a stalled scan. After the split j, recurse on the ranges specified by that implementation, not the final-pivot ranges of Lomuto.

Rule 40

CMU's middle-position pivot is a deterministic position choice, not a median-key oracle. Carefully arranged input can repeatedly make that position contain an extreme value. The lecture's partition variant must be traced with its own ≤ rule.

Rule 41

In randomized quicksort on distinct keys, ranks i<j are directly compared exactly when one endpoint is the first pivot from ranks i through j. Their comparison probability is 2/(j-i+1).

Rule 42

Summing the pair indicators gives expected comparisons 2(n+1)Hn-4n. This is an expectation over pivot randomness for a fixed distinct-key input. It is not an exact count for one observed trace.

Rule 43

Do not substitute the mean child size into a nonlinear recurrence. The correct expectation averages the costs for all possible pivot ranks. A distribution concentrated on extreme splits can have mean balanced child size and still quadratic expected work.

Rule 44

A random shuffle makes every distinct-key permutation equally likely when implemented correctly. It gives an expected guarantee, while a worst execution can still make quadratic comparisons. Probability and worst-case statements must remain separate.

Rule 45

Choosing the median of three distinct sampled keys excludes the sampled extremes, but does not ensure a constant-fraction split of the full array. The global pivot rank can still be close to an endpoint.

Rule 46

The median of a distinct sample of 2s+1 guarantees at least s smaller and s larger sampled keys. Thus both full children have at most n-s-1 keys. The sample-selection cost must be included in the recurrence.

Rule 47

A sample of 2n+1 keys sorted by insertion sort costs Θ(n) in its worst case. The most unbalanced allowed split yields T(n)=T(n-n)+T(n)+Θ(n) up to rounding, with order Θ(n3/2) under that worst-split model.

Rule 48

Recursing on the smaller quicksort child bounds stack space only if the larger child is handled by iteration or tail-call elimination. Making two ordinary recursive calls in a different order does not itself bound the maximum live recursion chain.

Rule 49

A Dutch-national-flag partition maintains less, equal, unknown, and greater regions. After swapping an unknown key with the right boundary, inspect the new key at the current index before advancing it.

Rule 50

Three-way quicksort omits the equal block from recursion. With a first-key pivot and one ternary comparison per remaining key, an all-equal input costs n-1 comparisons in one partition. Count Boolean tests separately if that is the requested operation.

Rule 51

A constant number r of distinct key values gives an O(nr) bound for the simple three-way recursion. A single frequent value does not force linear total work when the remaining records have many distinct keys.

Rule 52

Neither ordinary Lomuto nor ordinary three-way swapping is stable. Equal keys can move through swaps with unrelated keys. Adding an equal region improves duplicate handling, but does not automatically preserve original equal-key order.

Rule 53

In a zero-based binary heap, children are 2i+1,2i+2 and a nonroot parent is ⌊(i-1)/2⌋. The last internal node is ⌊n/2⌋-1. For n≤1, there is no internal node to sink.

Rule 54

Floyd construction processes internal nodes from bottom to top. Each child's subtree is already a heap when its parent is sunk. This direction is the inductive reason that one downward repair suffices.

Rule 55

Summing node heights proves Floyd construction linear: most nodes have small height. Multiplying n nodes by the root's height gives only an unnecessarily loose O(nlogn) bound.

Rule 56

Building a heap by repeated insertion is a different algorithm from Floyd construction. It can require Θ(nlogn) comparisons even though bottom-up construction is Θ(n). State which construction the question specifies.

Rule 57

During heapsort, the live heap occupies a prefix and the final sorted records occupy a suffix. After exchanging the root with the last live record, decrease the heap size before sinking. The sorted suffix must never be included in later repairs.

Rule 58

Heapsort is generally unstable because a root exchange can reverse equal identities. Its worst-case comparison cost is Θ(nlogn), but the stated early-stop sink can make all-equal input linear. Do not turn a worst-case bound into an every-input bound.

Rule 59

In a binary comparison decision tree for distinct keys, there are at least n! distinguishable orderings. Worst depth is at least ⌈log2(n!)⌉. A node with a three-outcome oracle requires a separately stated branching model.

Rule 60

A comparison lower bound does not prohibit linear best-case behavior. It says some distinct-key input requires the large depth for a correct general sorter. It also does not apply to a counting algorithm that exploits a restricted integer universe.

Rule 61

For known multiplicities m1,…,mr, the number of key-order arrangements is n!/∏jmj!. The binary information bound is its base-two logarithm. State whether labels must also be stably preserved and what information is given in advance.

Rule 62

Merging already sorted distinct runs needs only (p+qp) possible interleavings, not (p+q)!. Its information lower bound is therefore ⌈log2(p+qp)⌉. Ordinary head merging need not attain this bound on unequal run lengths.

Rule 63

Randomization cannot evade the general comparison information bound on expected comparisons averaged over uniformly distributed distinct-key permutations. Conditioning on the random choices yields deterministic trees; averaging preserves the lower bound.

Rule 64

Counting sort with key interval [L,H] uses K=H-L+1 counters. Its usual cost is Θ(n+K) and stable auxiliary storage is Θ(n+K). A large sparse key interval can dominate both even if only a few key values occur.

Rule 65

Frequency counts alone suffice to reconstruct sorted integer keys, but not arbitrary records with payloads. Stable counting sort scatters original records into an output array. The two versions solve different output contracts.

Rule 66

Prefix counts represent exclusive ends of key blocks. Scanning input from right to left, decrement the appropriate end and place the record there. This direction preserves original tie order.

Rule 67

With cumulative ends, a left-to-right scatter reverses ties. A left-to-right stable scatter instead uses starting positions and increments them. Direction and pointer meaning must be paired consistently.

Rule 68

A monotone shift k↦k-L preserves signed integer order and makes keys nonnegative. Sorting unsigned encodings of negative values without a corresponding monotone transformation can put negative keys after positive ones.

Rule 69

LSD radix sorting requires a stable sort at each digit. After t passes, records are ordered by the low t digits. An unstable later pass can destroy the lower-digit ordering established by earlier passes.

Rule 70

Sorting all records globally by the most significant digit and then globally by a less significant digit makes the later digit primary. MSD radix instead recurses within earlier digit buckets. These are different procedures.

Rule 71

If keys satisfy 0≤k<U, the digit count is ⌈logBU⌉ for U>1. If the maximum key is inclusively M, it is ⌊logBM⌋+1 for M>0. The difference matters exactly at powers of the base.

Rule 72

Compute digit counts by exact repeated integer division when implementation correctness matters. Dividing bit lengths is not a valid replacement for logarithms in an arbitrary base. For U=310, the maximum U-1 needs ten base-three digits.

Rule 73

Radix cost is Θ(d(n+B)) for d digit passes with counting-based digit sorting. A larger base reduces passes but increases counter initialization and storage. The best base depends on both the word width and the input size.

Rule 74

The word-RAM assumption must include digit extraction and integer arithmetic costs. If keys contain Θ(n) bits, reading all keys already requires quadratic bit volume. A constant-time unbounded-integer assumption cannot silently justify a bit-complexity claim.

Rule 75

FIFO distribution into digit buckets followed by concatenation is stable. Prepending to each bucket reverses local order unless it is reversed back appropriately. Check identity order at every pass, not only the final keys.

Rule 76

Bucket sorting is expected linear under suitable distribution and independence assumptions; its worst case can be quadratic with insertion-sorted buckets. Uniformity is an assumption about input generation, not a property obtained by drawing equal-width buckets.

Rule 77

With independent uniform assignment to B buckets, E[∑jNj2]=n+n(n-1)/B. This second-moment calculation explains the expected local quadratic work. Dependence or concentration can invalidate the conclusion.

Rule 78

For variable-length strings in MSD sorting, the end-of-string symbol precedes every real character. Otherwise a proper prefix can be put after its extension. Complexity must account for inspected characters and the representation of the alphabet.

Rule 79

Introsort uses a depth budget to replace pathological quicksort subproblems with heapsort. Small-subproblem insertion sorting adds a controlled cutoff cost. Its guarantee comes from the fallback and budget, rather than from a promise that all pivots are good.

Rule 80

For external merging, distinguish comparisons from block transfers. With memory M, block size B, and a feasible fan-in of approximately M/B-1, each full read/write pass costs about 2n/B transfers, subject to rounding and buffering overhead. Always state the memory reserved for output and metadata before fixing the exact fan-in.

21. Interactive sorting laboratory

Change the array, choose a precisely named variant, and inspect every comparison, move, held key, output buffer, pivot region or heap transition. Letters retain original identity. Playback starts paused. Previous, next, restart, seek, speed and keyboard controls are available. Reduced-motion mode preserves complete checkpoints without movement animation. Printing includes the state captions, counters and every checkpoint; answers remain complete text when animations cannot run.

Enter 1–10 integers from −999 to 999. Counting intervals may contain at most 24 keys. Radix uses a monotone shift of the minimum key, and a base from 2 to 10. Bucket keys must be integer percentages from 0 to 99. The displayed comparison convention is specified in the lesson; radix/counting distribution uses no key comparisons. An invalid submission preserves the last valid trace.
